questions.question: A client with heart failure has jugular venous distention and leg edema but also cool skin, confusion, weak pulses, and oliguria. Which interpretation is safest?
choices: The client may have both congestion and poor tissue perfusion
Edema proves cardiac output is adequate
Oliguria proves the client needs an immediate large fluid bolus
The findings show stable compensated heart failure
questions.explanation: Excess total-body fluid can coexist with low forward flow. Congestion plus cerebral, skin, and renal hypoperfusion requires urgent reassessment and escalation.

questions.question: A client suddenly becomes severely dyspneic, hypoxemic, diaphoretic, and unable to lie flat, with diffuse crackles and pink frothy sputum. What should the RN do first?
choices: Sit the client upright, activate emergency support, and begin ABC and oxygenation interventions
Encourage the client to walk to mobilize fluid
Lay the client flat for a complete examination
Delay intervention until the next daily weight
questions.explanation: This pattern suggests acute pulmonary edema. Upright positioning, emergency activation, oxygenation support, monitoring, and rapid prescribed therapy take priority.

questions.question: Which change most strongly suggests worsening congestion in a client with chronic heart failure?
choices: New orthopnea with rapid weight gain and increasing ankle edema
Stable weight and usual activity tolerance
Improved appetite with clear lungs
Unchanged blood pressure after morning medication
questions.explanation: Orthopnea, rapid weight gain, and increasing edema form a consistent congestion pattern and should be reported according to the individualized action plan.

questions.question: Which finding best demonstrates an effective response to prescribed IV loop-diuretic therapy for acute congestion?
choices: Less dyspnea and orthopnea, improved oxygenation, urine response, and reduced congestion without hypotension or severe electrolyte change
A larger urine volume despite worsening confusion and hypotension
New muscle weakness with falling potassium
Rising oxygen need with persistent crackles
questions.explanation: Effective decongestion improves symptoms and examination findings without causing dangerous perfusion, renal, or electrolyte harm.

questions.question: Which statement about HFpEF is accurate?
choices: Severe congestion can occur even though the ejection fraction is preserved
A preserved ejection fraction rules out heart failure
HFpEF never causes pulmonary edema
All HFrEF medications have identical benefits in HFpEF
questions.explanation: HFpEF commonly involves impaired filling and elevated pressure. EF classification does not measure the entire clinical syndrome or eliminate decompensation risk.

questions.question: Which cluster most strongly supports cardiogenic shock?
choices: Cool clammy skin, altered mentation, weak pulses, oliguria, hypotension, and pulmonary congestion
Warm dry skin with normal mentation and stable urine output
Isolated ankle edema after prolonged standing
Mild fatigue with normal perfusion and no respiratory change
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure with inadequate tissue perfusion and may coexist with pulmonary congestion. It requires emergency critical-care support and cause-directed treatment.

questions.question: Which medication groups form the usual four foundational classes for eligible clients with chronic symptomatic HFrEF?
choices: ARNI or appropriate ACE inhibitor/ARB, evidence-based beta blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor
Loop diuretic, antibiotic, opioid, and antihistamine
Aspirin, fibrinolytic, nitrate, and calcium supplement
NSAID, thiazolidinedione, decongestant, and corticosteroid
questions.explanation: The four foundational HFrEF classes target long-term outcomes. Diuretics relieve congestion but have a different role, and eligibility and monitoring are individualized.

questions.question: A client taking an ACE inhibitor and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist has new weakness, potassium 6.2 mEq/L, and peaked T waves. What is the priority?
choices: Initiate urgent hyperkalemia and cardiac-monitoring response and notify the treating team
Give the next doses before reporting the findings
Encourage a potassium-rich snack
Recheck the potassium at the next annual visit
questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG change is immediately life threatening. Heart-failure medications can contribute, so emergency stabilization and medication review are required.

questions.question: Which statement by a client shows correct understanding of home heart-failure monitoring?
choices: I will weigh myself under consistent conditions and follow my written plan for rapid weight gain or worsening symptoms
I only need to check my weight when my shoes no longer fit
I will double my diuretic whenever I feel tired without calling
If my ejection fraction improves, I can stop all medicines on my own
questions.explanation: Consistent daily trends and an individualized action threshold can identify congestion early. Medication changes should follow the authorized plan.

questions.question: Which symptom should a client with heart failure treat as an emergency rather than wait for a routine appointment?
choices: Severe shortness of breath at rest with new confusion and blue lips
Stable ability to complete usual activities
Unchanged mild ankle swelling at the established baseline
A planned medication refill due next month
questions.explanation: Severe rest dyspnea, altered mentation, and cyanosis indicate threatened oxygenation and perfusion and require emergency services.
